stem: A company needs to store millions of images and videos and serve them over the internet with high durability.

options.why: Instance store is temporary, which isn't what this scenario needs.
EFS is a shared file system for compute instances.
S3 is object storage designed for virtually unlimited data with 11 nines of durability.
EBS is block storage attached to EC2 instances.

explanation.answer: Amazon S3 stores data as objects in buckets, scales virtually without limit and is designed for 99.999999999% durability.
explanation.concept: S3 is commonly used for media, backups, data lakes and static websites.
explanation.examTip: Store lots of files/media durably = S3.

stem: An EC2 instance needs a persistent disk for its database files that survives instance stops.

options.why: EFS is a shared file system; the simplest persistent disk for one instance's database files is EBS.
Instance store data is lost when the instance stops.
Glacier is archival object storage, not a mounted disk.
EBS provides persistent block storage volumes for EC2.

explanation.answer: Amazon EBS provides persistent block-level storage volumes for EC2 instances, independent of the instance's lifecycle.
explanation.concept: EBS volumes live in one AZ; snapshots are stored in S3 for backup.
explanation.examTip: Persistent disk for EC2 = EBS.

stem: Several Linux EC2 instances across multiple AZs need to read and write the same files at the same time.

options.why: EFS is a shared, elastic NFS file system accessible from many instances across AZs.
Instance store is local and temporary, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.
Glacier is archival storage, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.
A standard EBS volume attaches to instances in one AZ, not shared across AZs.

explanation.answer: Amazon EFS is a serverless, elastic file system that many Linux instances can mount at the same time across AZs.
explanation.concept: EFS grows and shrinks automatically as files are added and removed.
explanation.examTip: Shared Linux file system across instances = EFS.

stem: A company runs Windows applications that need a shared file system with SMB and Active Directory integration.

options.why: S3 is object storage, not an SMB file share.

options.text: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server
options.why: FSx for Windows File Server provides fully managed Windows file shares with SMB and AD.
EBS is block storage for one instance at a time (in general).
EFS uses NFS for Linux workloads, which isn't what this scenario needs.

explanation.answer: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server provides fully managed shared storage built on Windows Server, with SMB and Active Directory support.
explanation.concept: The FSx family also includes Lustre, NetApp ONTAP and OpenZFS.
explanation.examTip: Windows SMB file shares = FSx for Windows File Server.

references.title: What is FSx for Windows File Server?

stem: A company stores log files that are accessed often for 30 days, then rarely, and must be deleted after one year.
prompt: What is the MOST cost-effective approach?

options.text: Delete the logs manually every week with a script
options.why: Manual or ad hoc deletion is error-prone and doesn't transition storage classes.

options.text: Keep all logs in S3 Standard indefinitely
options.why: This costs more and doesn't remove logs after a year.

options.text: Use S3 Lifecycle rules to transition and expire them
options.why: Lifecycle rules move objects to cheaper classes and delete them on schedule.

options.text: Store the logs on large EBS volumes instead
options.why: EBS is more expensive for logs and lacks lifecycle rules.

explanation.answer: S3 Lifecycle rules automatically transition objects to lower-cost storage classes and expire them after a set time.
explanation.concept: Common pattern: Standard → Standard-IA → Glacier → expire.
explanation.examTip: Move then delete on a schedule = S3 Lifecycle rules.

stem: A company has data with unknown and changing access patterns and wants storage costs optimized automatically.
prompt: Which S3 storage class fits BEST?

options.why: Deep Archive has long retrieval times and suits rarely accessed archives.
One Zone-IA stores data in one AZ and suits re-creatable, infrequently accessed data.
Standard doesn't optimize cost for infrequent access.
Intelligent-Tiering moves objects between access tiers automatically based on usage.

explanation.answer: S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves data to the most cost-effective access tier without performance impact or retrieval fees.
explanation.concept: It's ideal when access patterns are unknown or change over time.
explanation.examTip: Unknown access pattern = Intelligent-Tiering.

stem: A company must keep tax records for ten years and rarely, if ever, retrieve them. A 12-hour retrieval time is acceptable.
prompt: Which storage class is the LOWEST cost?

options.why: Deep Archive is the lowest-cost S3 storage class, with retrieval within hours.
Standard-IA costs more than archive classes.
Instant Retrieval gives millisecond access at a higher price than Deep Archive.
Intelligent-Tiering adds monitoring and costs more than Deep Archive for known cold data.

explanation.answer: S3 Glacier Deep Archive is the lowest-cost storage class for long-term retention, with retrieval typically within 12 hours.
explanation.concept: Pick archive classes based on how fast you'd need the data back.
explanation.examTip: Cheapest, rarely retrieved, hours OK = Glacier Deep Archive.

stem: A company wants to host a simple static marketing website (HTML, CSS, images) at low cost.

options.text: AWS Amplify Hosting with a build pipeline
options.why: Amplify can host static sites too, but S3 website hosting is the simplest option with no build setup.
S3 can serve static websites directly, often with CloudFront in front.
EBS is block storage for instances, which isn't what this scenario needs.

options.text: A fleet of EC2 instances behind a load balancer
options.why: This works but adds cost and management for static content.

explanation.answer: Amazon S3 can host static websites. Adding Amazon CloudFront provides HTTPS, caching and lower latency.
explanation.concept: No servers to manage for static content.
explanation.examTip: Static website = S3 (+ CloudFront).

references.title: Hosting a static website using Amazon S3

stem: A company wants point-in-time backups of its EBS volumes that can be used to create new volumes in another AZ.

options.why: Instance store is temporary and can't be snapshotted this way.
AWS Backup can manage EBS backups, but the underlying point-in-time copies are EBS snapshots.
EBS snapshots are stored durably and can restore volumes in any AZ in the Region.
This speeds uploads, which isn't what this scenario needs.

explanation.answer: EBS snapshots are incremental, point-in-time backups stored in Amazon S3. They can create new volumes in any AZ or be copied to other Regions.
explanation.concept: Use Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager or AWS Backup to automate snapshots.
explanation.examTip: Back up EBS = snapshots.

stem: A company wants one place to manage backup policies for EBS, RDS, DynamoDB, EFS and more, across accounts.

options.why: Storage Gateway connects on-premises apps to cloud storage; it doesn't manage backup policies across services.
Data Lifecycle Manager automates EBS snapshots and AMIs only, not RDS, DynamoDB and EFS.
DataSync transfers data; it isn't a backup policy manager.
AWS Backup centralizes and automates backups across AWS services.

explanation.answer: AWS Backup is a fully managed service to centralize and automate data protection across AWS services and hybrid workloads.
explanation.concept: Backup plans define frequency and retention; policies can be applied organization-wide.
explanation.examTip: Centralized backups across services = AWS Backup.

stem: A company wants on-premises applications to keep using file shares while the data is stored in Amazon S3.

options.why: Storage Gateway provides on-premises access to cloud storage, such as file shares backed by S3.
Snowball moves data offline in bulk, so it doesn't meet this requirement.
EFS is a file system for AWS compute, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.

options.text: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server
options.why: FSx provides file shares in AWS, but on-premises apps would need a network path; Storage Gateway caches locally and stores data in S3.

explanation.answer: AWS Storage Gateway is a hybrid cloud storage service that gives on-premises applications access to virtually unlimited cloud storage.
explanation.concept: Gateway types include S3 File Gateway, FSx File Gateway, Volume Gateway and Tape Gateway.
explanation.examTip: On-prem apps + cloud-backed storage = Storage Gateway.

stem: A company wants to replace its physical backup tapes but keep its existing backup software, which writes to tape.

options.why: DataSync transfers files; it doesn't emulate tape libraries.
Tape Gateway presents virtual tapes to backup software and stores them in S3 and Glacier.
Snapshots back up EBS, not on-premises tape workflows.
EFS is a file system, not a tape interface.

explanation.answer: Tape Gateway provides a virtual tape library that existing backup applications can use, with tapes archived to S3 Glacier classes.
explanation.concept: This removes physical tape handling without changing backup software.
explanation.examTip: Replace physical tapes, keep backup software = Tape Gateway.

stem: A team accidentally overwrote important files in an S3 bucket and wants to prevent permanent loss in the future.

options.why: Notifications report events but don't keep copies.
This optimizes cost, so it doesn't meet this requirement.
Versioning keeps previous versions of objects so overwrites and deletes can be recovered.
This speeds uploads, which isn't what this scenario needs.

explanation.answer: S3 Versioning keeps multiple versions of an object, allowing recovery from accidental overwrites and deletions.
explanation.concept: Combine with lifecycle rules to expire old versions and control cost.
explanation.examTip: Recover overwritten/deleted objects = S3 Versioning.

references.title: Retaining multiple versions of objects with S3 Versioning

stem: A company wants objects copied automatically from a bucket in one Region to a bucket in another Region for disaster recovery.

options.why: S3 Select queries data within objects, which isn't what this scenario needs.
Lifecycle rules change storage classes or delete objects.
Object Lambda transforms data on retrieval.
CRR automatically copies objects to a bucket in another Region.

explanation.answer: S3 Cross-Region Replication automatically and asynchronously copies new objects to a destination bucket in another Region.
explanation.concept: Versioning must be enabled on both buckets.
explanation.examTip: Copy objects to another Region automatically = Cross-Region Replication.

stem: A company asks how durable Amazon S3 Standard is designed to be.

options.why: S3 is designed for 11 nines of durability.
No storage system can rule out every possible loss.
This is far lower than S3's durability design.
That's closer to availability targets, not durability.

explanation.answer: Amazon S3 is designed for 99.999999999% (11 nines) durability by storing data redundantly across devices and facilities.
explanation.concept: Durability is about not losing data; availability is about being able to access it.
explanation.examTip: S3 durability = 11 nines.

stem: A company wants to attach an existing EBS volume to an instance in a different Availability Zone.

options.text: Convert the volume to instance store
options.why: Instance store can't be created from EBS.

options.text: Create a snapshot and restore a new volume in the other AZ
options.why: Snapshots can create volumes in any AZ in the Region.

options.text: Move the volume with AWS DataSync
options.why: DataSync doesn't move EBS volumes between AZs.

options.text: Attach it directly; EBS works across AZs
options.why: A volume can only attach to instances in its own AZ.

explanation.answer: EBS volumes are tied to one AZ. To use the data in another AZ, snapshot the volume and create a new volume from the snapshot there.
explanation.concept: Snapshots can also be copied to other Regions.
explanation.examTip: EBS is AZ-scoped; move via snapshots.

stem: A company stores thumbnail images that can be regenerated from originals and are accessed infrequently. It wants the lowest-cost option with millisecond access.
prompt: Which S3 storage class fits BEST?

options.why: Standard costs more for infrequently accessed data.
Express One Zone is for very high performance, not low-cost infrequent access.
One Zone-IA costs less by storing data in one AZ, fine for re-creatable data.
Deep Archive retrieval takes hours, so it doesn't meet this requirement.

explanation.answer: S3 One Zone-IA stores data in a single AZ at lower cost than Standard-IA. It suits infrequently accessed, re-creatable data.
explanation.concept: Data in One Zone classes can be lost if that AZ is destroyed.
explanation.examTip: Infrequent + re-creatable + cheap = One Zone-IA.

stem: Users around the world upload large files to one S3 bucket and complain that uploads are slow.
prompt: Which feature can speed up long-distance uploads?

options.why: Object Lock prevents deletion, which isn't what this scenario needs.
Versioning keeps object versions, so it doesn't meet this requirement.
Lifecycle rules manage storage classes, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.
Transfer Acceleration routes uploads through CloudFront edge locations over the AWS network.

explanation.answer: S3 Transfer Acceleration uses edge locations to speed up transfers over long distances to an S3 bucket.
explanation.concept: Multipart upload also helps with large files.
explanation.examTip: Faster long-distance uploads to S3 = Transfer Acceleration.

references.title: Configuring fast transfers using S3 Transfer Acceleration

stem: A company is choosing storage for three needs: a boot disk for EC2, a shared Linux file system and a data lake of files.

options.text: EBS for the boot disk, EFS for the shared file system, S3 for the data lake
options.why: Each service matches its storage type: block, file and object.
Instance store is temporary and not shared.

options.text: EFS for the boot disk, S3 for the shared file system, EBS for the data lake
options.why: These mappings don't fit how the services work.

options.text: S3 for the boot disk, EBS for the shared file system, EFS for the data lake
options.why: These mappings don't fit how the services work.

explanation.answer: EBS = block storage for instances. EFS = shared file storage. S3 = object storage for data lakes and files at scale.
explanation.concept: Block, file and object storage serve different access patterns.
explanation.examTip: Block=EBS, File=EFS/FSx, Object=S3.

stem: A remote mining site with poor connectivity needs to collect sensor data, process it locally and later ship it to AWS.

options.why: Outposts needs a reliable connection to its AWS Region, which the site doesn't have.
Snowball Edge provides local storage and compute at disconnected sites and can be shipped to AWS.
Storage Gateway needs a network connection to AWS and doesn't provide local compute for a disconnected site.
EFS requires network access to AWS, so it doesn't meet this requirement.

explanation.answer: AWS Snowball Edge devices offer storage and compute for edge locations with limited connectivity, then ship data to AWS.
explanation.concept: Snowball Edge is used for offline transfer and edge processing.
explanation.examTip: Disconnected site + local compute + ship data later = Snowball Edge.

stem: A hospital stores medical images that are rarely accessed but must be available within milliseconds when a doctor requests them.
prompt: Which storage class is MOST cost-effective?

options.why: Standard costs more for rarely accessed data.
Deep Archive retrieval takes hours, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.
Instant Retrieval offers archive pricing with millisecond access.
Flexible Retrieval takes minutes to hours.

explanation.answer: S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval is for long-lived, rarely accessed data that still needs millisecond retrieval.
explanation.concept: Compare Glacier classes by retrieval speed: Instant (ms), Flexible (minutes–hours), Deep Archive (hours).
explanation.examTip: Rarely accessed but needed instantly = Glacier Instant Retrieval.

stem: A company is choosing services to move data into AWS.
prompt: Which TWO services are designed for data transfer? (Select TWO.)

options.why: Glacier is a storage class, not a transfer service.
EFS is a file system destination, not a data transfer service.
Snowball Edge transfers data offline with physical devices.
AWS Backup protects data already in AWS; it isn't a tool for moving data into AWS.
DataSync transfers data online between storage systems and AWS.

explanation.answer: DataSync (online) and Snowball Edge (offline) are AWS data transfer services. Storage Gateway and Transfer Family also move data.
explanation.concept: Choose online transfer when bandwidth allows; offline for very large volumes.
explanation.examTip: Online = DataSync. Offline = Snowball.

stem: A company's partners send files using SFTP. It wants those files to land directly in Amazon S3 without running its own SFTP servers.

options.why: EFS is a file system, not an SFTP endpoint.
SNS sends notifications, which isn't what this scenario needs.
CloudFront delivers content, which isn't what this scenario needs.
Transfer Family provides managed SFTP, FTPS and FTP endpoints backed by S3 or EFS.

explanation.answer: AWS Transfer Family provides fully managed file transfer endpoints (SFTP, FTPS, FTP, AS2) that store data in Amazon S3 or Amazon EFS.
explanation.concept: Partners keep their existing tools while you avoid managing servers.
explanation.examTip: Managed SFTP into S3 = Transfer Family.

stem: A research team runs high-performance computing jobs that need a very fast parallel file system linked to data in Amazon S3.

options.why: FSx for Lustre is a high-performance parallel file system that can link to S3.

options.text: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server
options.why: This is for Windows SMB workloads, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.
Deep Archive is for cold archives, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.
Cold HDD is low-cost, low-performance block storage.

explanation.answer: Amazon FSx for Lustre provides a high-performance file system for HPC, ML and media processing, with S3 integration.
explanation.concept: It delivers very high throughput and low latency.
explanation.examTip: HPC parallel file system = FSx for Lustre.

references.title: What is Amazon FSx for Lustre?

stem: A new user asks how data is organized in Amazon S3.

options.text: Data is stored in folders on a shared NFS mount
options.why: That describes EFS, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.

options.text: Data is stored as objects in buckets, each identified by a key
options.why: S3 stores objects in buckets, which matches what the question asks for.

options.text: Data is stored in tables with rows and columns
options.why: That describes relational databases, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.

options.text: Data is stored as blocks on volumes attached to instances
options.why: That describes EBS, which isn't what this scenario needs.

explanation.answer: S3 stores data as objects inside buckets. Each object has a key (name), data and metadata.
explanation.concept: Bucket names are globally unique; buckets are created in a Region.
explanation.examTip: S3 = buckets + objects + keys.
